issues.description: req.stream vs req.bounded_stream change complects WSGI/ASGI transport with example logic without explanation
issues.detail: The example silently switches body reading from req.stream to req.bounded_stream. These have different time semantics: stream is the raw, possibly-unbounded socket; bounded_stream respects Content-Length. That's a real fact about the world (how many bytes constitute this request), and the change is load-bearing for the new test, yet nothing in the example names why. The value (the body bytes) and the identity (which stream object) are being conflated in the reader's head.

issues.description: FAQ example complects header overrides with a contrived handler that re-reads Content-Length to fake a 400
issues.detail: The PostTest handler reads req.stream.read(req.content_length or 0) and returns 400 when the body is empty-but-length-nonzero. That is not a property of Falcon; it is the example fabricating the behavior it claims to demonstrate. The actual lesson (you can override headers in simulate_post) is one line; the rest is incidental scaffolding that teaches the wrong mental model of where the 400 comes from.

issues.description: The new test asserts a 400 that depends on a quietly-changed implementation detail, not on a documented contract
issues.detail: resp4 expects 400 for empty body with Content-Length: 1. That outcome exists only because the example was switched to bounded_stream in this same PR. The test is therefore testing the test setup, not a behavior of the example or the framework. The essential question (what should Falcon do when Content-Length lies?) is never named; the test just pins the current accident.

issues.description: README diff bundles unrelated cosmetic reformatting with a behavior change (str status to code_to_http_status, handle signature reorder)
issues.detail: Two concerns are intertwined in one diff: docs reflow (blank lines, line-wrapping, %-format to .format) and real semantic edits (StorageError.handle parameter order, resp.status construction, stream to bounded_stream). Reviewers cannot cheaply separate the value-changing edits from the typographic ones. These are different facts about the world and want different commits.

issues.description: Test bundles three independent assertions into one function, complecting unrelated cases
issues.detail: test_things_advanced now asserts GET, two GETs after POST, a successful POST, and a malformed-length POST in one function with shared mutable app state. Each case is a distinct fact; a failure in resp3 will mask resp4 and vice versa. Splitting into named tests makes each value (request, response, expectation) standalone and the time order between them explicit only where it actually matters.

issues.description: The question that should have been asked first: what is the contract when Content-Length disagrees with the body?
issues.detail: Before adding a test, sit in the hammock: is a lying Content-Length a client error the example should reject, a transport-layer concern Falcon already handles, or undefined behavior? The PR picks an answer by accident (bounded_stream returns empty, handler raises 400) without stating the contract. Name the contract, then the test and the code follow trivially; skip it and you've pinned an accident as policy.

review.summary: This PR is a small, reasonable test addition wrapped around an unstated semantic change (req.stream to req.bounded_stream) and a FAQ example that fabricates the behavior it claims to teach. The real fact about the world — what should happen when Content-Length disagrees with the actual body — is never named, so the new assertions pin an incidental outcome rather than an essential contract. The README diff additionally complects cosmetic reflow with behavior changes, making the value-bearing edits hard to see. Decompose: (1) name the Content-Length contract in prose, (2) make the stream/bounded_stream switch its own commit with a one-line rationale, (3) split the omnibus test into one assertion per fact, (4) shrink the FAQ example to the one line that demonstrates header override and drop the contrived handler. Hammock first; the keyboard work then becomes obvious and small.
